//! Bounded single-producer/single-consumer input queues for device IRQ paths.
//!
//! Each queue has one producer (its device IRQ handler) and one consumer on the
//! bootstrap CPU. Producers never wait or allocate; full queues drop the newest
//! byte and increment a saturating overflow counter.

use core::sync::atomic::{AtomicU8, AtomicUsize, Ordering};

pub const INPUT_QUEUE_CAPACITY: usize = 256;

pub static UART_INPUT: ByteRing<INPUT_QUEUE_CAPACITY> = ByteRing::new();
pub static KEYBOARD_INPUT: ByteRing<INPUT_QUEUE_CAPACITY> = ByteRing::new();
pub static INPUT_EVENT_PENDING: core::sync::atomic::AtomicBool =
    core::sync::atomic::AtomicBool::new(false);

/// A fixed-capacity SPSC queue. Its producer and consumer must remain unique.
pub struct ByteRing<const CAPACITY: usize> {
    bytes: [AtomicU8; CAPACITY],
    head: AtomicUsize,
    tail: AtomicUsize,
    head_index: AtomicUsize,
    tail_index: AtomicUsize,
    overflows: AtomicUsize,
}

impl<const CAPACITY: usize> ByteRing<CAPACITY> {
    pub const fn new() -> Self {
        Self {
            bytes: [const { AtomicU8::new(0) }; CAPACITY],
            head: AtomicUsize::new(0),
            tail: AtomicUsize::new(0),
            head_index: AtomicUsize::new(0),
            tail_index: AtomicUsize::new(0),
            overflows: AtomicUsize::new(0),
        }
    }

    /// Push without waiting. Returns false when the queue is full.
    pub fn try_push(&self, byte: u8) -> bool {
        if CAPACITY == 0 {
            self.increment_overflows();
            return false;
        }
        let head = self.head.load(Ordering::Relaxed);
        let tail = self.tail.load(Ordering::Acquire);
        if head.wrapping_sub(tail) >= CAPACITY {
            self.increment_overflows();
            return false;
        }
        let index = self.head_index.load(Ordering::Relaxed);
        self.bytes[index].store(byte, Ordering::Relaxed);
        self.head_index
            .store(self.next_index(index), Ordering::Relaxed);
        self.head.store(head.wrapping_add(1), Ordering::Release);
        true
    }

    /// Pop one byte if available; this never waits.
    pub fn try_pop(&self) -> Option<u8> {
        if CAPACITY == 0 {
            return None;
        }
        let tail = self.tail.load(Ordering::Relaxed);
        let head = self.head.load(Ordering::Acquire);
        if tail == head {
            return None;
        }
        let index = self.tail_index.load(Ordering::Relaxed);
        let byte = self.bytes[index].load(Ordering::Relaxed);
        self.tail_index
            .store(self.next_index(index), Ordering::Relaxed);
        self.tail.store(tail.wrapping_add(1), Ordering::Release);
        Some(byte)
    }

    pub fn overflow_count(&self) -> usize {
        self.overflows.load(Ordering::Acquire)
    }

    pub fn is_empty(&self) -> bool {
        self.head.load(Ordering::Acquire) == self.tail.load(Ordering::Acquire)
    }

    fn next_index(&self, index: usize) -> usize {
        if index == CAPACITY - 1 {
            0
        } else {
            index + 1
        }
    }

    fn increment_overflows(&self) {
        let _ = self
            .overflows
            .try_update(Ordering::Relaxed, Ordering::Relaxed, |count| {
                Some(count.saturating_add(1))
            });
    }
}

impl<const CAPACITY: usize> Default for ByteRing<CAPACITY> {
    fn default() -> Self {
        Self::new()
    }
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::ByteRing;
    use core::assert_eq;
    use core::sync::atomic::Ordering;

    #[test]
    fn bounded_queue_preserves_order_and_reports_overflow() {
        let queue = ByteRing::<3>::new();
        assert!(queue.is_empty());
        assert!(queue.try_push(b'a'));
        assert!(queue.try_push(b'b'));
        assert!(queue.try_push(b'c'));
        assert!(!queue.try_push(b'd'));
        assert_eq!(queue.overflow_count(), 1);
        assert_eq!(queue.try_pop(), Some(b'a'));
        assert!(queue.try_push(b'd'));
        assert_eq!(queue.try_pop(), Some(b'b'));
        assert_eq!(queue.try_pop(), Some(b'c'));
        assert_eq!(queue.try_pop(), Some(b'd'));
        assert_eq!(queue.try_pop(), None);
        assert!(queue.is_empty());
    }

    #[test]
    fn non_power_of_two_capacity_survives_counter_wraparound() {
        let queue = ByteRing::<3>::new();
        queue.head.store(usize::MAX, Ordering::Relaxed);
        queue.tail.store(usize::MAX, Ordering::Relaxed);

        assert!(queue.try_push(b'a'));
        assert!(queue.try_push(b'b'));
        assert!(queue.try_push(b'c'));
        assert_eq!(queue.try_pop(), Some(b'a'));
        assert!(queue.try_push(b'd'));
        assert_eq!(queue.try_pop(), Some(b'b'));
        assert_eq!(queue.try_pop(), Some(b'c'));
        assert_eq!(queue.try_pop(), Some(b'd'));
        assert_eq!(queue.try_pop(), None);
    }

    #[test]
    fn zero_capacity_queue_fails_without_dividing_or_waiting() {
        let queue = ByteRing::<0>::new();
        assert!(!queue.try_push(1));
        assert_eq!(queue.try_pop(), None);
        assert_eq!(queue.overflow_count(), 1);
    }
}

# Claude Code instructions for Rustix

These are project-specific instructions for Claude Code and Claude-based agents working in this repository. `AGENTS.md` is the canonical shared engineering contract; read and follow it together with this file. If advice conflicts, preserve the stricter Rustix safety and validation rule, and do not infer that an unfinished subsystem is complete.

## What this repository is

Rustix is an experimental 64-bit Unix-like operating system with its own Rust kernel. The kernel is `no_std` and targets `x86_64-unknown-none`. Limine is only the external boot protocol/loader. Do not conflate the loader with Rustix or describe a host tool as the kernel.

The project is deliberately staged. Rustix currently boots to a kernel-mode Crabshell over COM1, with bounded IRQ input and a volatile RAM filesystem. A single-vCPU cooperative runtime handles shell waits; this is not a userspace terminal, persistent filesystem, secure shell, or POSIX implementation. The `crabshell` workspace crate parses commands only; kernel I/O and filesystem operations remain in the kernel.

## Status must stay honest

Before planning a task, read `docs/roadmap/README.md` and the relevant architecture document. Milestones 0–3 have met their documented local exit criteria; the source includes:

- A Limine handoff and fixed-capacity owned boot snapshot with structural validation, CPUID/address-width reporting, and a classified memory map.
- A bounded physical-frame allocator, cloned active page-table hierarchy, kernel-image HHDM permission hardening, and a fixed BSS heap with bounded frame-backed growth.
- Bootstrap GDT/TSS/IDT and fatal exception stubs for vectors 0–31; double faults use an IST stack, and page faults report CR2/error bits.
- A validated single-vCPU xAPIC/I/O APIC path with masked-first IRQ routes, PIT ticks, EOI handling, and bounded UART/PS/2 IRQ input.
- A single-vCPU cooperative thread runtime and a separate allocation-free Crabshell parser with a bounded volatile RAM filesystem.

Important limitations:

- Milestone 0–3 validation evidence is documented in `AGENTS.md` and `docs/roadmap/README.md`; it does not validate uncommitted changes in the current working tree.
- Structural boot checks cannot prove that a non-null Limine pointer is readable; the loader trust boundary remains.
- Scheduling is cooperative, not preemptive. There is no SMP, userspace, syscall ABI, persistent storage, user/kernel isolation, or general-purpose device model.
- Exceptions remain fatal-only. The shell and VFS run in ring 0 and are not isolated or secure.

Do not check off roadmap criteria merely because code or an interface exists. Only report builds, tests, and emulator checks that you actually ran and observed passing.

## Required workflow

1. Read `AGENTS.md`, the relevant `docs/architecture/*.md` document, and the actual implementation/call sites before changing code.
2. Identify the subsystem boundary and failure behavior. For hardware work, state assumptions about privilege level, selectors, page mappings, stack state, and IF/interrupt state before coding.
3. Make the smallest coherent vertical change. Prefer tested architecture-independent helpers in `src/lib.rs` modules over untestable freestanding-only logic when that preserves the design.
4. Add or update tests for normal, boundary, malformed, and exhaustion cases. Keep parser tests in `crates/crabshell`; do not make that crate depend on kernel facilities.
5. Update the relevant architecture, testing, security, and roadmap docs in the same change.
6. Run the narrow validation first, then the broader check appropriate to the touched paths.
7. In the final summary, distinguish implementation from verification and list any environmental blocker or remaining risk.

Do not commit, create branches, run broad formatting rewrites, or modify unrelated files unless explicitly requested.

## Rustix implementation rules

### `no_std` and fixed capacity

- Kernel code must remain freestanding and `no_std`; use `core`, not `std`.
- Avoid new Rust dependencies unless there is a concrete need and compatibility/security review.
- There is no general heap. Do not add `Vec`, `String`, `Box`, or allocation-dependent interfaces to kernel paths.
- Fixed-capacity tables must document capacity, exhaustion behavior, and whether an error leaves state unchanged.
- The kernel binary is not the host test target. Keep pure logic in the `rustix-kernel` library where practical.

### Boot, memory, and physical frames

- Limine writes response pointers before `_start`; response-bearing request records and their linker section must remain writable to the loader.
- Validate pointer nullness/alignment/counts and checked arithmetic, but preserve the documented trust boundary: Rustix cannot prove a loader pointer is mapped and readable.
- All physical ranges are half-open `[start, end)`. Use checked arithmetic and reject overlaps rather than silently normalizing malformed maps.
- Only `RegionKind::Usable` ranges feed the frame allocator. Reserved, ACPI, loader-reclaimable, framebuffer, bad, executable/module, and unknown ranges are never ordinary free frames.
- A frame handle represents a physical address; it is not a pointer. Do not dereference it, add the HHDM offset and assume success, or change CR3 until a reviewed mapping policy proves the access and ownership.
- The active page tables are currently inherited from Limine. Any future replacement must preserve the executing kernel, boot stack, `BootInfo`, request/response objects, GDT/TSS/IDT data, exception stacks, and all mappings needed for continued execution.
- The current allocator is bounded and single-owner/single-core. It is not a page-table manager, heap, or concurrent allocator.

### x86_64 and exceptions

- Keep privileged instructions, port I/O, assembly, and raw pointer operations in narrow architecture modules with nearby safety comments.
- The current GDT/TSS/IDT path is fatal-only. It does not initialize a PIC/APIC, enable maskable interrupts, recover from faults, or provide a general IRQ subsystem.
- Do not add `sti`, exception recovery, preemption, or claims of interrupt support without an explicit design, ownership/locking rules, fault injection, and emulator validation.
- When editing `src/arch/x86_64/interrupts.rs`, review normalized CPU-error-code stack layout, register-save ordering, stack alignment before calling Rust, the double-fault IST, descriptor selectors, and fatal behavior. Assembly diagnostics are not a substitute for assembling/linking the target.
- `CPUID` support bits do not prove a feature is enabled in control registers or active page tables. Label reports as supported/capable unless activation is verified.

### Crabshell and VFS

- The parser crate may contain syntax/model types, but no terminal, VFS, kernel, or hardware I/O.
- Kernel command execution belongs in `src/shell.rs`; the fixed-capacity VFS contract belongs in `src/vfs.rs`.
- RAM filesystem contents disappear on reset. Preserve explicit errors, root protection, directory rules, path limits, node limits, and file-size limits.
- When adding/changing a command, update parser behavior/tests, shell execution/help, `docs/architecture/crabshell.md`, and user-facing examples as appropriate.

## Supported validation

Run these from the repository root using `just`:

```sh
just fmt
just test
just check
just build
just image
just smoke
just verify
```

`just test` runs host tests for memory-map validation, frame allocator behavior, VFS, and Crabshell parsing. `just check` type-checks `x86_64-unknown-none`; `just build` links the release ELF. `just verify` covers formatting, host tests, target check, pinned Limine image creation, and bounded QEMU prompt smoke. Image/boot steps need Python 3, `xorriso`, QEMU, the target, and network access for the first pinned download.

Changes to boot requests/entry, `linker.ld`, `src/arch/x86_64/`, memory allocation, paging, or heap code should receive `just verify` when the environment permits. If it does not, report the exact command failure and leave the corresponding roadmap criterion unchecked.

Editor diagnostics are useful but are not proof that Rust compiled, assembly assembled, the target linked, the image booted, or the hardware path works. Never say “tests pass” when they were not run.

## Relevant documentation

- `docs/index.md` — documentation entry point and current status.
- `docs/roadmap/README.md` — sequencing and milestone exit criteria.
- `docs/architecture/overview.md` — architecture and subsystem layering.
- `docs/architecture/boot.md` — Limine request/response contract and trust boundary.
- `docs/architecture/memory.md` — ranges, frame allocator, inherited mappings, and future paging.
- `docs/architecture/crabshell.md` — parser, commands, and RAM filesystem contract.
- `docs/architecture/drivers.md` — driver status and scope.
- `docs/security.md` — unsafe boundaries and security requirements.
- `docs/development/building.md`, `docs/development/testing.md` — commands and evidence expectations.

# Gemini CLI instructions for Rustix

This file provides project-specific context for Gemini CLI and Gemini-based coding agents. Read `AGENTS.md` before editing; it is the canonical shared contract for all agents. Also follow any more specific instructions attached to the user request. Do not weaken the safety, status, or validation requirements described here and in `AGENTS.md`.

## Project identity and goal

Rustix (Rust-unix) is an experimental 64-bit Unix-like operating system with its own Rust kernel. The kernel itself is built as a `no_std` binary for `x86_64-unknown-none`. Limine is an external boot protocol/loader, not the Rustix kernel. A Python standard-library script only builds and smoke-tests the boot image; it does not implement OS behavior.

The project aims toward Unix-like services incrementally. It does not currently claim POSIX conformance, security isolation, or production readiness. Unsupported operations should produce clear failures or be documented as future work, not silently approximated.

## Current state and validation boundaries

Milestones 0–3 have met their documented local exit criteria. The repository has a Limine boot path, validated boot snapshot and memory map, CPUID reporting, a bounded physical-frame allocator, cloned active page tables, a bounded global heap, bootstrap GDT/TSS/IDT exception handling, a validated single-vCPU xAPIC/I/O APIC and PIT path, cooperative scheduling, Crabshell, and a volatile fixed-capacity RAM filesystem.

Crabshell's parser is a standalone allocation-free `no_std` workspace crate. Kernel-side I/O and command execution are in `src/shell.rs`. Shell input uses bounded COM1 IRQ input with polling fallback; PS/2 IRQ input remains raw scancode reporting. The shell runs in ring 0 and is not a userspace application or a POSIX shell. `meminfo` reports validated RAM and frame counts. The bounded heap and frame-backed mappings are kernel services, but allocation is not allowed in IRQ/exception context.

Do not assume uncommitted source is validated just because a previous tree passed:

- Milestone 0–3 evidence is recorded in `AGENTS.md` and `docs/roadmap/README.md`; rerun relevant checks for current changes.
- Structural boot validation cannot prove that a non-null Limine pointer is readable; this remains a loader trust boundary.
- Scheduling is single-vCPU and cooperative, not timer-preemptive. Exceptions remain fatal-only. There is no SMP, userspace, syscall ABI, persistent storage, user/kernel isolation, or general-purpose device model.

Never mark a roadmap item complete merely because an API, design, or source file exists. The relevant implementation and validation evidence must both meet that item's exit criteria.

## How to work in this repository

1. Start at the repository root. Read `AGENTS.md`, the relevant architecture document, and the actual implementation and call sites before making changes.
2. Keep the task scoped. Prefer a small, coherent, testable vertical slice; avoid speculative scaffolding or broad rewrites.
3. Identify invariants, capacity limits, failure semantics, and any unsafe boundary before coding.
4. Put architecture-independent logic in the `rustix-kernel` library when appropriate so host tests can exercise it. Keep the freestanding binary and parser crate boundaries intact.
5. Add or update tests and documentation together. If code and docs disagree, inspect the implementation and resolve the mismatch in the same change.
6. Run the narrowest relevant validation, then broaden it. Record exact commands and actual results.
7. Report files changed, behavior delivered, validation observed, and remaining risks. Do not conceal failures or say a check passed if it did not run.

Do not commit, create branches, alter project history, or modify unrelated files unless the user explicitly requests it.

## Rust, dependencies, and API constraints

- Keep kernel and OS implementation code `no_std`; use `core` rather than `std` in the kernel.
- Do not add a third-party Rust dependency without a concrete need and compatibility/security review. The existing project uses in-tree abstractions.
- No general heap exists. Avoid `alloc`-dependent interfaces, `Vec`, `String`, and `Box` in kernel services unless the task explicitly implements and validates the allocator first.
- Fixed-capacity data structures must document their limit, exhaustion/error behavior, and mutation guarantees on failure.
- Keep `crates/crabshell` limited to parsing and command representation. It must not depend on the VFS, kernel modules, serial I/O, or hardware.
- Treat `src/lib.rs` as the host-testable architecture-independent kernel library boundary; the freestanding binary is not a host test target.

## Memory, boot, and safety constraints

- Limine writes the response pointers into request records before entering `_start`; those records must remain in writable loaded storage.
- The boot snapshot checks pointer nullness/alignment, count limits, checked arithmetic, physical range validity, and overlap. It cannot establish that loader-provided memory is mapped/readable; the Limine handoff remains a trust boundary.
- Physical regions use half-open `[start, end)` ranges. Use checked arithmetic for every endpoint and address calculation.
- Feed only `Usable` regions to the frame allocator. Never turn ACPI, loader-reclaimable, reserved, framebuffer, bad-memory, executable/module, or unknown classifications into free frames without an explicit ownership transition.
- A frame is a physical address, not a dereferenceable pointer. HHDM access is restricted to checked full-frame, allocator-token paths that rely on the documented Limine contract. Do not access arbitrary physical addresses or change page-table ownership without a reviewed mapping and lifetime proof.
- Limine currently supplies the active page tables. Replacing them must preserve the executing kernel image, bootstrap stack, `BootInfo`, request/response memory, GDT/TSS/IDT, exception stacks, and required direct-map/console mappings.
- The current frame allocator has fixed range metadata and is not a heap, page mapper, concurrent allocator, or scheduling primitive.

## x86_64 hardware and exception rules

- Keep port I/O, privileged instructions, raw pointer operations, and assembly isolated under `src/arch/x86_64/` and document their invariants near each unsafe block.
- Exception vectors 0–31 remain fatal-only; double faults use an IST stack, and page faults report CR2 and error bits. The validated single-vCPU APIC path enables only configured, registered IRQ routes after dispatch and EOI setup.
- The PIT timer handler only increments ticks and acknowledges the local APIC; it does not preempt threads. Do not broaden IRQ use or add preemption/SMP without explicit ownership and synchronization rules, tests, and emulator validation.
- When modifying exception stubs, verify CPU error-code normalization, stack layout, saved-register order, SysV stack alignment before calling Rust, GDT selectors, TSS descriptor/IST setup, and non-returning failure behavior.
- CPUID capability bits indicate support, not necessarily that a feature is enabled in CR registers or active paging.
- Hardware/boot code changes require more than host unit tests: include target check/build and emulator validation when possible. If unavailable, describe the exact blocker and keep status unverified.

## Crabshell and filesystem contract

- Crabshell is a kernel-mode serial shell with a separate parser crate; it is not a process or a security boundary.
- The RAM filesystem is volatile, bounded, and reset on reboot. It has no persistent block device, permissions, links, journaling, or general POSIX semantics.
- Preserve explicit path, capacity, and mutation errors. Do not add hidden truncation or destructive overwrite behavior.
- When adding a command, update parser syntax/tests, kernel execution/help, and `docs/architecture/crabshell.md`; update README examples if users will encounter it.

## Supported repository checks

Run commands from the repository root:

```sh
just fmt
just test
just check
just build
just image
just smoke
just verify
```

- `just fmt` checks workspace Rust formatting.
- `just test` runs host-side ACPI, paging, frame allocator, heap, IRQ/time/input/scheduler policy, VFS, and Crabshell parser tests.
- `just check` checks the freestanding `x86_64-unknown-none` target; it is not a final link.
- `just build` links the optimized kernel ELF.
- `just image` builds the hybrid ISO and may download the pinned Limine archive on first use.
- `just smoke` uses QEMU and checks that the shell prompt is reached.
- `just verify` combines formatting, host tests, target check, image creation, BIOS/OVMF boot, active-map, cooperative-thread, and UART/PS/2 input smokes.

Image and boot checks need Python 3, `xorriso`, QEMU, the Rust target, and network access for the initial pinned download. For changes to boot entry/requests, linker configuration, architecture code, frame allocation, paging, or heap code, the intended full validation is `just verify`. Report failed or unavailable commands exactly. Editor diagnostics are not a substitute for Cargo or QEMU evidence.

## Documentation to consult

- `docs/index.md` — project status and documentation map.
- `docs/roadmap/README.md` — milestone plan and exit criteria.
- `docs/architecture/overview.md` — architecture and layering.
- `docs/architecture/boot.md` — Limine handoff and boot snapshot.
- `docs/architecture/memory.md` — physical ranges, frame allocation, and paging direction.
- `docs/architecture/crabshell.md` — parser, shell commands, and RAM filesystem.
- `docs/architecture/drivers.md` — implemented drivers and limitations.
- `docs/security.md` — unsafe boundaries and security requirements.
- `docs/development/building.md` and `docs/development/testing.md` — build/test workflows and evidence policy.

     6	Rustix (Rust-unix) is an experimental, 64-bit, Unix-like operating system whose kernel is written in Rust. This repository builds the kernel itself; Limine is used only as the external boot protocol/loader, not as a substitute for a Rustix kernel.
     7	
     8	Rustix now boots into **Crabshell**, a small kernel-mode shell on the COM1 serial terminal. It includes basic navigation and file commands backed by a fixed-capacity RAM filesystem.     10	## Quick start
    11

    13

    19	just test

    29

The RAM filesystem holds at most 31 entries plus its root, with files capped at 1024 bytes.     56	
    57	The grammar intentionally does not yet support quoted paths, escaped quotes, variables, pipes, redirection, globbing, command substitution, history, or a process launcher. Input is a single ASCII line (up to 256 bytes) from the serial port.
    58	
    59	## RAM filesystem contract
    60	
    61	- The root plus at most 31 live entries fit in the fixed 32-node table.
    62	- Path components are limited to 31 UTF-8 bytes; file contents are limited to 1024 bytes each.
    63	- Paths may be absolute or relative and support repeated `/`, `.`, and `..`.
    64	- `write` replaces a file; `append` adds bytes; `touch` never truncates. Oversized path-based writes and appends fail before creating a missing file, and failed capacity checks leave existing contents unchanged.
    65	- `cp` copies files and replaces an existing destination file. `mv` moves files only and refuses to overwrite an existing destination. `rm` handles files only. `rmdir` refuses non-empty directories and the current directory.
    66	- Filesystem allocation is fixed-capacity; errors are reported rather than allocating a heap.
    67	- Every file and directory disappears when the machine resets. There is no block device, journaling, metadata persistence, permission model, links, or concurrent access yet.
    68	
    69	## Tests and limitations
    70	
    71	Host-side tests cover path traversal, file create/write/append/copy/move/remove, entry kinds, path rendering, directory emptiness, capacity failures without namespace mutation, and the parser's syntax/arity. The automated QEMU smoke test checks that the serial shell reaches its prompt. A separate manual `just run` session exercised `help`, `ls`, `meminfo`, `mkdir`, `cd`, `touch`, `write`, `append`, `cat`, `cp`, `mv`, `rm`, `rmdir`, and `pwd`; `cat` returned the appended text, `cp` replaced an existing destination with source contents, `rmdir` refused a nonempty directory, and `pwd` returned to `/home/rustix` after cleanup. The unsupported `memtest` command produced the expected unknown-command response. These checks do not emulate reboot persistence, exhaustively test shell interactions, or prove isolation. Since the shell runs in ring 0, a parser or filesystem bug can panic the entire kernel. This implementation must not be presented as a secure or POSIX-compliant shell.

# Claude Code instructions for Rustix

These are project-specific instructions for Claude Code and Claude-based agents working in this repository. `AGENTS.md` is the canonical shared engineering contract; read and follow it together with this file. If advice conflicts, preserve the stricter Rustix safety and validation rule, and do not infer that an unfinished subsystem is complete.

## What this repository is

Rustix is an experimental 64-bit Unix-like operating system with its own Rust kernel. The kernel is `no_std` and targets `x86_64-unknown-none`. Limine is only the external boot protocol/loader. Do not conflate the loader with Rustix or describe a host tool as the kernel.

The project is deliberately staged. Rustix currently boots to a kernel-mode Crabshell over COM1, with bounded IRQ input and a volatile RAM filesystem. A single-vCPU cooperative runtime handles shell waits; this is not a userspace terminal, persistent filesystem, secure shell, or POSIX implementation. The `crabshell` workspace crate parses commands only; kernel I/O and filesystem operations remain in the kernel.

## Status must stay honest

Before planning a task, read `docs/roadmap/README.md` and the relevant architecture document. Milestones 0–3 have met their documented local exit criteria; the source includes:

- A Limine handoff and fixed-capacity owned boot snapshot with structural validation, CPUID/address-width reporting, and a classified memory map.
- A bounded physical-frame allocator, cloned active page-table hierarchy, kernel-image HHDM permission hardening, and a fixed BSS heap with bounded frame-backed growth.
- Bootstrap GDT/TSS/IDT and fatal exception stubs for vectors 0–31; double faults use an IST stack, and page faults report CR2/error bits.
- A validated single-vCPU xAPIC/I/O APIC path with masked-first IRQ routes, PIT ticks, EOI handling, and bounded UART/PS/2 IRQ input.
- A single-vCPU cooperative thread runtime and a separate allocation-free Crabshell parser with a bounded volatile RAM filesystem.

Important limitations:

- Milestone 0–3 validation evidence is documented in `AGENTS.md` and `docs/roadmap/README.md`; it does not validate uncommitted changes in the current working tree.
- Structural boot checks cannot prove that a non-null Limine pointer is readable; the loader trust boundary remains.
- Scheduling is cooperative, not preemptive. There is no SMP, userspace, syscall ABI, persistent storage, user/kernel isolation, or general-purpose device model.
- Exceptions remain fatal-only. The shell and VFS run in ring 0 and are not isolated or secure.

Do not check off roadmap criteria merely because code or an interface exists. Only report builds, tests, and emulator checks that you actually ran and observed passing.

## Required workflow

1. Read `AGENTS.md`, the relevant `docs/architecture/*.md` document, and the actual implementation/call sites before changing code.
2. Identify the subsystem boundary and failure behavior. For hardware work, state assumptions about privilege level, selectors, page mappings, stack state, and IF/interrupt state before coding.
3. Make the smallest coherent vertical change. Prefer tested architecture-independent helpers in `src/lib.rs` modules over untestable freestanding-only logic when that preserves the design.
4. Add or update tests for normal, boundary, malformed, and exhaustion cases. Keep parser tests in `crates/crabshell`; do not make that crate depend on kernel facilities.
5. Update the relevant architecture, testing, security, and roadmap docs in the same change.
6. Run the narrow validation first, then the broader check appropriate to the touched paths.
7. In the final summary, distinguish implementation from verification and list any environmental blocker or remaining risk.

Do not commit, create branches, run broad formatting rewrites, or modify unrelated files unless explicitly requested.

## Rustix implementation rules

### `no_std` and fixed capacity

- Kernel code must remain freestanding and `no_std`; use `core`, not `std`.
- Avoid new Rust dependencies unless there is a concrete need and compatibility/security review.
- The global heap is bounded: a 256 KiB BSS arena plus up to 1 MiB of frame-backed growth. Allocation remains forbidden in IRQ/exception context; prefer fixed-capacity interfaces for core paths.
- Fixed-capacity tables must document capacity, exhaustion behavior, and whether an error leaves state unchanged.
- The kernel binary is not the host test target. Keep pure logic in the `rustix-kernel` library where practical.

### Boot, memory, and physical frames

- Limine writes response pointers before `_start`; response-bearing request records and their linker section must remain writable to the loader.
- Validate pointer nullness/alignment/counts and checked arithmetic, but preserve the documented trust boundary: Rustix cannot prove a loader pointer is mapped and readable.
- All physical ranges are half-open `[start, end)`. Use checked arithmetic and reject overlaps rather than silently normalizing malformed maps.
- Only `RegionKind::Usable` ranges feed the frame allocator. Reserved, ACPI, loader-reclaimable, framebuffer, bad, executable/module, and unknown ranges are never ordinary free frames.
- A frame handle represents a physical address; it is not a pointer. Do not dereference it, add the HHDM offset and assume success, or change CR3 until a reviewed mapping policy proves the access and ownership.
- The active root is an allocator-owned clone of Limine's reachable hierarchy. Any future replacement must preserve the executing kernel, boot stack, `BootInfo`, request/response objects, GDT/TSS/IDT data, exception stacks, and all mappings needed for continued execution.
- The current allocator is bounded and single-owner/single-core. It is not a page-table manager, heap, or concurrent allocator.

### x86_64 and exceptions

- Keep privileged instructions, port I/O, assembly, and raw pointer operations in narrow architecture modules with nearby safety comments.
- Exception handling remains fatal-only. The validated single-vCPU APIC path enables only configured, registered routes after IRQ dispatch and EOI setup; the timer IRQ does not preempt or switch contexts.
- Do not broaden IRQ use, add exception recovery, preemption, or SMP without an explicit design, ownership/locking rules, fault injection, and emulator validation.
- When editing `src/arch/x86_64/interrupts.rs`, review normalized CPU-error-code stack layout, register-save ordering, stack alignment before calling Rust, the double-fault IST, descriptor selectors, and fatal behavior. Assembly diagnostics are not a substitute for assembling/linking the target.
- `CPUID` support bits do not prove a feature is enabled in control registers or active page tables. Label reports as supported/capable unless activation is verified.

### Crabshell and VFS

- The parser crate may contain syntax/model types, but no terminal, VFS, kernel, or hardware I/O.
- Kernel command execution belongs in `src/shell.rs`; the fixed-capacity VFS contract belongs in `src/vfs.rs`.
- RAM filesystem contents disappear on reset. Preserve explicit errors, root protection, directory rules, path limits, node limits, and file-size limits.
- When adding/changing a command, update parser behavior/tests, shell execution/help, `docs/architecture/crabshell.md`, and user-facing examples as appropriate.

## Supported validation

Run these from the repository root using `just`:

```sh
just fmt
just test
just check
just build
just image
just smoke
just verify
```

`just test` runs host tests for ACPI parsing, paging and mapping policy, frame allocation, heap, IRQ/time/input/scheduler policy, VFS, and Crabshell parsing. `just check` type-checks `x86_64-unknown-none`; `just build` links the release ELF. `just verify` covers formatting, host tests, target check, pinned Limine image creation, BIOS/OVMF boot, active-map, cooperative-thread, and UART/PS/2 input QEMU smokes. Image/boot steps need Python 3, `xorriso`, QEMU, OVMF, the target, and network access for the first pinned download.

Changes to boot requests/entry, `linker.ld`, `src/arch/x86_64/`, memory allocation, paging, or heap code should receive `just verify` when the environment permits. If it does not, report the exact command failure and leave the corresponding roadmap criterion unchecked.

Editor diagnostics are useful but are not proof that Rust compiled, assembly assembled, the target linked, the image booted, or the hardware path works. Never say “tests pass” when they were not run.

## Relevant documentation

- `docs/index.md` — documentation entry point and current status.
- `docs/roadmap/README.md` — sequencing and milestone exit criteria.
- `docs/architecture/overview.md` — architecture and subsystem layering.
- `docs/architecture/boot.md` — Limine request/response contract and trust boundary.
- `docs/architecture/memory.md` — ranges, frame allocator, inherited mappings, and future paging.
- `docs/architecture/crabshell.md` — parser, commands, and RAM filesystem contract.
- `docs/architecture/drivers.md` — driver status and scope.
- `docs/security.md` — unsafe boundaries and security requirements.
- `docs/development/building.md`, `docs/development/testing.md` — commands and evidence expectations.

# Gemini CLI instructions for Rustix

This file provides project-specific context for Gemini CLI and Gemini-based coding agents. Read `AGENTS.md` before editing; it is the canonical shared contract for all agents. Also follow any more specific instructions attached to the user request. Do not weaken the safety, status, or validation requirements described here and in `AGENTS.md`.

## Project identity and goal

Rustix (Rust-unix) is an experimental 64-bit Unix-like operating system with its own Rust kernel. The kernel itself is built as a `no_std` binary for `x86_64-unknown-none`. Limine is an external boot protocol/loader, not the Rustix kernel. A Python standard-library script only builds and smoke-tests the boot image; it does not implement OS behavior.

The project aims toward Unix-like services incrementally. It does not currently claim POSIX conformance, security isolation, or production readiness. Unsupported operations should produce clear failures or be documented as future work, not silently approximated.

## Current state and validation boundaries

Milestones 0–3 have met their documented local exit criteria. The repository has a Limine boot path, validated boot snapshot and memory map, CPUID reporting, a bounded physical-frame allocator, cloned active page tables, a bounded global heap, bootstrap GDT/TSS/IDT exception handling, a validated single-vCPU xAPIC/I/O APIC and PIT path, cooperative scheduling, Crabshell, and a volatile fixed-capacity RAM filesystem.

Crabshell's parser is a standalone allocation-free `no_std` workspace crate. Kernel-side I/O and command execution are in `src/shell.rs`. Shell input uses bounded COM1 IRQ input with polling fallback; PS/2 IRQ input remains raw scancode reporting. The shell runs in ring 0 and is not a userspace application or a POSIX shell. `meminfo` reports validated RAM and frame counts. The bounded heap and frame-backed mappings are kernel services, but allocation is not allowed in IRQ/exception context.

Do not assume uncommitted source is validated just because a previous tree passed:

- Milestone 0–3 evidence is recorded in `AGENTS.md` and `docs/roadmap/README.md`; rerun relevant checks for current changes.
- Structural boot validation cannot prove that a non-null Limine pointer is readable; this remains a loader trust boundary.
- Scheduling is single-vCPU and cooperative, not timer-preemptive. Exceptions remain fatal-only. There is no SMP, userspace, syscall ABI, persistent storage, user/kernel isolation, or general-purpose device model.

Never mark a roadmap item complete merely because an API, design, or source file exists. The relevant implementation and validation evidence must both meet that item's exit criteria.

## How to work in this repository

1. Start at the repository root. Read `AGENTS.md`, the relevant architecture document, and the actual implementation and call sites before making changes.
2. Keep the task scoped. Prefer a small, coherent, testable vertical slice; avoid speculative scaffolding or broad rewrites.
3. Identify invariants, capacity limits, failure semantics, and any unsafe boundary before coding.
4. Put architecture-independent logic in the `rustix-kernel` library when appropriate so host tests can exercise it. Keep the freestanding binary and parser crate boundaries intact.
5. Add or update tests and documentation together. If code and docs disagree, inspect the implementation and resolve the mismatch in the same change.
6. Run the narrowest relevant validation, then broaden it. Record exact commands and actual results.
7. Report files changed, behavior delivered, validation observed, and remaining risks. Do not conceal failures or say a check passed if it did not run.

Do not commit, create branches, alter project history, or modify unrelated files unless the user explicitly requests it.

## Rust, dependencies, and API constraints

- Keep kernel and OS implementation code `no_std`; use `core` rather than `std` in the kernel.
- Do not add a third-party Rust dependency without a concrete need and compatibility/security review. The existing project uses in-tree abstractions.
- The global heap is bounded: a 256 KiB BSS arena plus up to 1 MiB of frame-backed growth. Allocation is forbidden in IRQ/exception context; prefer fixed-capacity interfaces for core paths.
- Fixed-capacity data structures must document their limit, exhaustion/error behavior, and mutation guarantees on failure.
- Keep `crates/crabshell` limited to parsing and command representation. It must not depend on the VFS, kernel modules, serial I/O, or hardware.
- Treat `src/lib.rs` as the host-testable architecture-independent kernel library boundary; the freestanding binary is not a host test target.

## Memory, boot, and safety constraints

- Limine writes the response pointers into request records before entering `_start`; those records must remain in writable loaded storage.
- The boot snapshot checks pointer nullness/alignment, count limits, checked arithmetic, physical range validity, and overlap. It cannot establish that loader-provided memory is mapped/readable; the Limine handoff remains a trust boundary.
- Physical regions use half-open `[start, end)` ranges. Use checked arithmetic for every endpoint and address calculation.
- Feed only `Usable` regions to the frame allocator. Never turn ACPI, loader-reclaimable, reserved, framebuffer, bad-memory, executable/module, or unknown classifications into free frames without an explicit ownership transition.
- A frame is a physical address, not a dereferenceable pointer. HHDM access is restricted to checked full-frame, allocator-token paths that rely on the documented Limine contract. Do not access arbitrary physical addresses or change page-table ownership without a reviewed mapping and lifetime proof.
- The active page-table root is an allocator-owned clone of Limine's reachable hierarchy. Any future replacement must preserve the executing kernel image, bootstrap stack, `BootInfo`, request/response memory, GDT/TSS/IDT, exception stacks, and required direct-map/console mappings.
- The current frame allocator has fixed range metadata and is not a heap, page mapper, concurrent allocator, or scheduling primitive.

## x86_64 hardware and exception rules

- Keep port I/O, privileged instructions, raw pointer operations, and assembly isolated under `src/arch/x86_64/` and document their invariants near each unsafe block.
- Exception vectors 0–31 remain fatal-only; double faults use an IST stack, and page faults report CR2 and error bits. The validated single-vCPU APIC path enables only configured, registered IRQ routes after dispatch and EOI setup.
- The PIT timer handler only increments ticks and acknowledges the local APIC; it does not preempt threads. Do not broaden IRQ use or add preemption/SMP without explicit ownership and synchronization rules, tests, and emulator validation.
- When modifying exception stubs, verify CPU error-code normalization, stack layout, saved-register order, SysV stack alignment before calling Rust, GDT selectors, TSS descriptor/IST setup, and non-returning failure behavior.
- CPUID capability bits indicate support, not necessarily that a feature is enabled in CR registers or active paging.
- Hardware/boot code changes require more than host unit tests: include target check/build and emulator validation when possible. If unavailable, describe the exact blocker and keep status unverified.

## Crabshell and filesystem contract

- Crabshell is a kernel-mode serial shell with a separate parser crate; it is not a process or a security boundary.
- The RAM filesystem is volatile, bounded, and reset on reboot. It has no persistent block device, permissions, links, journaling, or general POSIX semantics.
- Preserve explicit path, capacity, and mutation errors. Do not add hidden truncation or destructive overwrite behavior.
- When adding a command, update parser syntax/tests, kernel execution/help, and `docs/architecture/crabshell.md`; update README examples if users will encounter it.

## Supported repository checks

Run commands from the repository root:

```sh
just fmt
just test
just check
just build
just image
just smoke
just verify
```

- `just fmt` checks workspace Rust formatting.
- `just test` runs host-side ACPI, paging, frame allocator, heap, IRQ/time/input/scheduler policy, VFS, and Crabshell parser tests.
- `just check` checks the freestanding `x86_64-unknown-none` target; it is not a final link.
- `just build` links the optimized kernel ELF.
- `just image` builds the hybrid ISO and may download the pinned Limine archive on first use.
- `just smoke` uses QEMU and checks that the shell prompt is reached.
- `just verify` combines formatting, host tests, target check, image creation, BIOS/OVMF boot, active-map, cooperative-thread, and UART/PS/2 input smokes.

Image and boot checks need Python 3, `xorriso`, QEMU, the Rust target, and network access for the initial pinned download. For changes to boot entry/requests, linker configuration, architecture code, frame allocation, paging, or heap code, the intended full validation is `just verify`. Report failed or unavailable commands exactly. Editor diagnostics are not a substitute for Cargo or QEMU evidence.

## Documentation to consult

- `docs/index.md` — project status and documentation map.
- `docs/roadmap/README.md` — milestone plan and exit criteria.
- `docs/architecture/overview.md` — architecture and layering.
- `docs/architecture/boot.md` — Limine handoff and boot snapshot.
- `docs/architecture/memory.md` — physical ranges, frame allocation, and paging direction.
- `docs/architecture/crabshell.md` — parser, shell commands, and RAM filesystem.
- `docs/architecture/drivers.md` — implemented drivers and limitations.
- `docs/security.md` — unsafe boundaries and security requirements.
- `docs/development/building.md` and `docs/development/testing.md` — build/test workflows and evidence policy.

# Rustix

> [!Note]
> **Yes**. This project is pretty much 100% AI coded. If you don't like or support AI, feel free to leave. 

Rustix (Rust-unix) is an experimental, 64-bit, Unix-like operating system whose kernel is written in Rust. This repository builds the kernel itself; Limine is used only as the external boot protocol/loader, not as a substitute for a Rustix kernel.

Rustix now boots into **Crabshell**, a small kernel-mode shell on the COM1 serial terminal. It includes basic navigation and file commands backed by a fixed-capacity RAM filesystem. The filesystem is volatile and reset at every boot; this is an early kernel shell, not a userspace process or POSIX shell. The command parser lives in a separate, allocation-free `crabshell` crate so a future GUI terminal can reuse it. Single-vCPU cooperative scheduling and bounded UART/PS/2 IRQ input are present; timer preemption, process isolation, persistent storage, a syscall ABI, networking, and userspace remain future work. See [`docs/roadmap/README.md`](docs/roadmap/README.md) for the staged plan.

## Quick start

Prerequisites: a Rust stable toolchain, `just`, Python 3, `xorriso`, QEMU (`qemu-system-x86_64`), and the target installed by `rust-toolchain.toml` (or `rustup target add x86_64-unknown-none`). The first image build downloads a pinned Limine binary release and verifies its SHA-256.

For a ready-to-use environment with these tools installed, open the repository in a Dev Container using `.devcontainer/`. The container uses Ubuntu 24.04 and includes the Rust target and `rustfmt` component from `rust-toolchain.toml`.

```sh
just help
just fmt
just test
just check
just build
just image
just smoke
just run       # interactive serial shell in QEMU; exit with Ctrl+C
just verify
```

`just build` produces `target/x86_64-unknown-none/release/rustix`. `just image` creates `target/rustix.iso`, a hybrid BIOS/UEFI image; `just smoke` checks that Crabshell reaches its prompt; and `just run` starts an interactive QEMU session attached to the current terminal.

Try `pwd`, `ls /`, `mkdir notes`, `write notes/hello.txt "hello from Rustix"`, `cat notes/hello.txt`, and `cd ..` in Crabshell. Commands include `help`, `clear`, `pwd`, `meminfo`, `ls`, `cd`, `mkdir`, `touch`, `write`, `append`, `cp`, `mv`, `cat`, `rm`, and `rmdir`. The RAM filesystem holds at most 31 entries plus its root, with files capped at 1024 bytes. See [`docs/architecture/crabshell.md`](docs/architecture/crabshell.md) for the shell and filesystem contract, [`docs/development/building.md`](docs/development/building.md) for build/emulator details, and [`docs/index.md`](docs/index.md) for the documentation map.

## Project principles

- The kernel and operating-system implementation are Rust-first and `no_std`; architecture-specific privileged operations are isolated under `src/arch/`.
- The kernel is the product. A bootloader may initialize the machine and transfer control, but policy, memory management, scheduling, and Unix-like services belong to Rustix.
- Keep unsafe code small, documented, and adjacent to its hardware/protocol boundary.
- Build incrementally: every roadmap milestone should have build checks, tests where practical, and updated design documentation.
- Unix-like behavior is an explicit compatibility goal, not a claim of POSIX compliance today.

## Repository map

- `src/main.rs` — freestanding kernel entry point and Crabshell handoff.
- `src/shell.rs` — serial line editor and kernel command executor.
- `src/vfs.rs` — fixed-capacity volatile RAM filesystem, with host-side tests.
- `crates/crabshell/` — separate `no_std` command parser crate; no I/O or filesystem coupling.
- `src/boot.rs` — mutable Limine response requests, validated owned boot snapshot, and diagnostics.
- `src/arch/x86_64/serial.rs` — COM1 formatted output, early polling input, and bounded IRQ RX queue.
- `src/arch/x86_64/cpu.rs` — baseline CPUID vendor and feature reporting.
- `src/arch/x86_64/interrupts.rs` — bootstrap GDT/TSS/IDT, fatal exception diagnostics, and IRQ entry/dispatch.
- `src/arch/x86_64/keyboard.rs` — bounded PS/2 IRQ scancode queue and non-blocking polling fallback.
- `src/arch/x86_64/apic.rs` — validated single-vCPU xAPIC/I/O APIC routing and PIT ticks.
- `src/arch/x86_64/context.rs` — cooperative x86_64 context-switch assembly.
- `src/arch/x86_64/io.rs` — narrow x86 port-I/O wrappers.
- `src/memory.rs` — fixed-capacity validated physical-memory-map snapshot and host tests.
- `src/frame.rs` — bounded physical frame allocator initialized from `BootInfo`; paging, heap growth, and guarded thread stacks use allocator-issued frames.
- `src/acpi.rs` — bounded ACPI table validation and MADT parsing helpers.
- `src/heap.rs` — fixed-capacity global heap policy and host tests.
- `src/input.rs` — bounded SPSC input queues and IRQ-to-scheduler event signaling.
- `src/irq.rs` — host-tested IRQ vector allocation policy.
- `src/kernel_threads.rs` — cooperative kernel-thread runtime and guarded-stack lifecycle.
- `src/paging.rs` — validated page-table cloning, mappings, and cache policy.
- `src/scheduler.rs` — host-tested cooperative scheduling and wait-queue policy.
- `src/time.rs` — PIT divisor and monotonic tick arithmetic.
- `.cargo/config.toml`, `linker.ld` — x86_64-none code generation and ELF layout.
- `justfile` — formatting, tests, target checks, image creation, emulator smoke test, and aggregate verification.
- `limine.conf` — pinned boot configuration for the Rustix kernel.
- `scripts/boot.py` — checksum-verified Limine download, hybrid ISO assembly, and bounded QEMU validation.
- `.github/workflows/ci.yml` — runs `just verify` on pushes and pull requests.
- `docs/` — architecture, drivers, development, security, and roadmap documentation.

# Crabshell and the early RAM filesystem

Crabshell is Rustix's first command-line interface. The current implementation is a **kernel-mode bootstrap shell** attached to COM1, not a separate user process. Its command parser is isolated in a separate crate so the same grammar can later be reused by a graphical terminal frontend or by a userspace terminal application.

## Crate boundary

- `crates/crabshell` is an allocation-free `no_std` Rust library. It parses a borrowed command line into a `Command` value and performs no I/O, filesystem access, scheduling, or privilege changes.
- `src/shell.rs` adapts the parser to the kernel serial driver, provides a small line editor, implements commands, and owns the current working-directory node.
- `src/vfs.rs` is a fixed-capacity in-memory filesystem used by the early shell. It is not a disk filesystem and is not persistent.

This is a useful separation now: future terminal frontends can reuse parsing without importing kernel hardware or filesystem code. A future user-mode Crabshell should keep its frontend/parser layer but execute operations through a documented syscall/VFS interface; it must not link the kernel's internal filesystem as a privilege shortcut.

## Build and run

```sh
just test
just image
just smoke
just run
```

`just run` starts a headless QEMU machine and connects the guest serial port to the current terminal. Use `Ctrl+C` in the host terminal to stop QEMU. The BIOS/UEFI boot image is `target/rustix.iso`.

The kernel welcomes the user in `/home/rustix`. The initial namespace contains `/bin`, `/dev`, `/etc`, `/home/rustix`, `/tmp`, and `/var`; `/etc/motd` explains that storage is volatile.

## Commands

| Command | Behavior |
|---|---|
| `help` | List available commands and limits. |
| `clear` | Send the ANSI clear-screen/home sequence. |
| `pwd` | Print the absolute working directory. |
| `ls [PATH]` | List a directory; a file path prints that file's name and size. Defaults to the current directory. |
| `cd PATH` | Change to an existing directory. Supports absolute and relative paths, `.`, and `..`. |
| `mkdir PATH` | Create one directory; its parent must already exist. |
| `touch PATH` | Create an empty file, or leave an existing file unchanged. |
| `write PATH TEXT` | Create a file if needed and replace its contents with the remaining line. Matching outer single or double quotes around the text are removed. |
| `append PATH TEXT` | Create a file if needed and append the remaining line. |
| `cp SOURCE DEST` | Copy a file; an existing destination file is replaced. |
| `mv SOURCE DEST` | Move/rename a file; directories and existing destinations are rejected. |
| `cat PATH` | Print a UTF-8 text file. Binary data is not displayed. |
| `rm PATH` | Remove a file. Directories are rejected. |
| `rmdir PATH` | Remove an empty directory other than the current directory. |

Example:

```text
root@rustix:/home/rustix# mkdir notes
root@rustix:/home/rustix# write notes/hello.txt "hello from Rustix"
root@rustix:/home/rustix# cat notes/hello.txt
hello from Rustix
root@rustix:/home/rustix# cd ..
root@rustix:/home# pwd
/home
```

The grammar intentionally does not yet support quoted paths, escaped quotes, variables, pipes, redirection, globbing, command substitution, history, or a process launcher. Input is a single ASCII line (up to 256 bytes) from COM1's bounded IRQ queue, with polling fallback; PS/2 IRQ bytes are reported as raw scancodes rather than translated into characters. A scancode diagnostic redraws the prompt and any partially typed line.

## RAM filesystem contract

- The root plus at most 31 live entries fit in the fixed 32-node table.
- Path components are limited to 31 UTF-8 bytes; file contents are limited to 1024 bytes each.
- Paths may be absolute or relative and support repeated `/`, `.`, and `..`.
- `write` replaces a file; `append` adds bytes; `touch` never truncates. Oversized path-based writes and appends fail before creating a missing file, and failed capacity checks leave existing contents unchanged.
- `cp` copies files and replaces an existing destination file. `mv` moves files only and refuses to overwrite an existing destination. `rm` handles files only. `rmdir` refuses non-empty directories and the current directory.
- Filesystem allocation is fixed-capacity; errors are reported rather than allocating a heap.
- Every file and directory disappears when the machine resets. There is no block device, journaling, metadata persistence, permission model, links, or concurrent access yet.

## Tests and limitations

Host-side tests cover path traversal, file create/write/append/copy/move/remove, entry kinds, path rendering, directory emptiness, capacity failures without namespace mutation, and the parser's syntax/arity. The automated QEMU smoke test checks that the serial shell reaches its prompt; `just input-smoke` additionally exercises UART/PS/2 IRQ wakeup and raw scancode reporting. A separate manual `just run` session exercised `help`, `ls`, `meminfo`, `mkdir`, `cd`, `touch`, `write`, `append`, `cat`, `cp`, `mv`, `rm`, `rmdir`, and `pwd`; `cat` returned the appended text, `cp` replaced an existing destination with source contents, `rmdir` refused a nonempty directory, and `pwd` returned to `/home/rustix` after cleanup. The unsupported `memtest` command produced the expected unknown-command response. These checks do not emulate reboot persistence, exhaustively test shell interactions, or prove isolation. Since the shell runs in ring 0, a parser or filesystem bug can panic the entire kernel. This implementation must not be presented as a secure or POSIX-compliant shell.

# Testing and verification

## Current checks

`just verify` runs the standard development verification sequence:

1. `just fmt` — fail on formatting differences across the workspace.
2. `just test` — run host-side ACPI parser/traversal, borrowed-page mapping, IRQ vector allocator, PIT rate/time arithmetic, memory-map, mapping-range/PTE-bit policy, frame-allocator, RAM-filesystem, and Crabshell parser tests.
3. `just check` — check the `x86_64-unknown-none` kernel target.
4. `just smoke` — build the pinned hybrid ISO, boot it in QEMU's default BIOS mode, and check that Crabshell reaches its prompt within a deadline.
5. `just uefi-smoke` — boot the same ISO with OVMF and require the copied MADT report, CR3/page-table transition and TLB-flush markers, timer IRQ delivery/EOI, and shell prompt within a deadline.
6. `just active-map-smoke` and `just thread-smoke` — exercise active owned-page mapping/TLB invalidation and (under OVMF) cooperative switching, event wakeup, timed sleep while another ready thread repeatedly yields, guarded stacks, and frame-backed heap growth; both restore the default image.
7. `just input-smoke` — under OVMF, send a shell command over UART and inject a PS/2 key through QMP; require the blocked shell to wake and report the raw scancode. The QMP socket is created under the host temporary directory because WSL `/mnt/c` does not support Unix sockets.

`just frame-smoke` builds an opt-in kernel variant that allocates one `Usable` frame, validates its HHDM address, writes and reads the whole page, clears it, returns it, and checks the prompt in QEMU. It reads the inherited root, walks all pages in the kernel image segments and requested 256 KiB stack span, compares effective PAT/MTRR types for kernel-image/HHDM aliases, and exercises a separate candidate map/unmap/release. The normal boot path in this image also clones the full reachable inherited hierarchy, hardens kernel-image HHDM aliases to text/rodata R/NX and data RW/NX while retaining PAT bits, switches CR3 with active-PCID and global-TLB invalidation, verifies the active root and critical mappings, and exercises the global heap's alignment, reuse, and deterministic exhaustion. The smoke test requires a serial marker confirming the applicable TLB invalidation path. The workflow restores the default release kernel and ISO. These probes rely on Limine's HHDM contract and do not inventory every unrelated mapping or prove physical-hardware correctness. `just fault-smoke` separately builds opt-in kernel variants that deliberately trigger a page fault and an invalid opcode. It requires each QEMU run to report the expected exception (and CR2 for the page fault), avoid the shell prompt, and remain halted until timeout. It then rebuilds and restores the default release kernel and ISO. These are fatal-path diagnostics, not exception recovery tests; diagnostic Cargo features are disabled by default and mutually exclusive.

Heap tests cover alignment, exact-layout free/reuse, zero-sized rejection, metadata exhaustion, and arena exhaustion. Tests reject malformed state, unsupported discontinuous masks, invalid indexes/ranges, out-of-range addresses, mismatched physical widths, and non-normal caching mode. The pure inherited-table walker does not access hardware tables; the opt-in QEMU reader and candidate backend use checked HHDM addresses. Boot-time QEMU checks a subset of live kernel/HHDM aliases but does not inventory all aliases or prove complete transition safety. Boot separately captures the registers and CR0 caching mode read-only and reports a diagnostic resolution; this is not a page-table or mapping test. The GDT/TSS/IDT and CPU-register paths are privileged kernel code. The temporary ACPI CR3/map/copy/restore path is hardware-only. QEMU boot and fault-injection checks complement, but do not replace, static review and target builds. Add tests for boundaries and failure behavior when introducing new pure kernel helpers. The kernel binary is not a host test target.

`just uefi-smoke` locates combined OVMF firmware or a matching CODE/VARS pair in standard system directories. `just thread-smoke` uses an opt-in kernel-thread probe, checks its completion marker, and restores the default release image. Split firmware uses a fresh temporary copy of the VARS template. `just input-smoke` validates UART RX and PS/2 IRQ delivery/wakeup against the normal default kernel. The OVMF checks require the expected MADT report and CR3-transition markers; install the Ubuntu `ovmf` package if no firmware is found. The BIOS smoke remains separate: if firmware places the RSDT in Reserved memory, the kernel's ACPI validation is expected to fail closed rather than accepting that table span.

## What current checks do not prove

- `cargo check` does not perform a final target link.
- A successful ELF link does not prove the boot protocol is recognized or `_start` is reached.
- Host unit tests do not validate privileged instructions, UART behavior, memory-map pointer validity, page tables, interrupts, or actual hardware. - The automated QEMU prompt smoke test asserts the cloned CR3 transition, the applicable active-PCID/global-TLB invalidation marker, kernel HHDM alias permissions/cache preservation, heap probe, and shell prompt. The clone preserves Limine's complete reachable hierarchy, but there is no clean-room mapping policy or exhaustive audit of unrelated aliases; emulator tests do not establish physical-hardware behavior. `just fault-smoke` exercises only the controlled page-fault and invalid-opcode fatal paths; it does not test every exception vector or recovery.
- A separate manual QEMU session exercised directory navigation and file create/write/append/read/copy/move/remove operations, including `cp` replacing an existing destination and rejection of `rmdir` on a nonempty directory. This is not exhaustive shell coverage and does not prove persistence across reboot.
- There is no on-disk filesystem integration test, syscall/userspace test, fuzz target, or physical-hardware test.

## Validation policy

For changes to the kernel entry, linker script, boot requests, architecture code, shell, or VFS, run `just verify`. For memory-management and ABI code, add negative tests for overflow, malformed ranges, permission failures, and invalid user pointers before exposing those paths to userspace.

Record commands actually run and any environment limitation in change summaries; never call an unexecuted build “passing.”

//! Bootstrap GDT, TSS, and interrupt entry for x86_64.
//!
//! Bootstrap installs exception and device-IRQ gates with maskable interrupts
//! disabled. APIC setup, route masking, handler registration, and explicit `sti`
//! are owned by the boot path; exceptions remain fatal-only.

use core::arch::{asm, global_asm};
use core::mem::size_of;

const EXCEPTION_COUNT: usize = 32;
const IRQ_FIRST_VECTOR: usize = 0x20;
const IRQ_LAST_VECTOR: usize = 0xef;
const IRQ_VECTOR_COUNT: usize = IRQ_LAST_VECTOR - IRQ_FIRST_VECTOR + 1;
const APIC_SPURIOUS_VECTOR: usize = 0xff;
const IRQ_STUB_COUNT: usize = IRQ_VECTOR_COUNT + 1;
const _: [(); 208] = [(); IRQ_VECTOR_COUNT];
const KERNEL_CODE_SELECTOR: u16 = 0x08;
const STACK_SIZE: usize = 16 * 1024;
const TSS_DESCRIPTOR_TYPE: u64 = 0x89;

#[repr(C, packed)]
struct DescriptorTablePointer {
    limit: u16,
    base: u64,
}

#[repr(C, align(16))]
struct IdtTable([IdtEntry; 256]);

#[repr(C, packed)]
#[derive(Clone, Copy)]
struct IdtEntry {
    offset_low: u16,
    selector: u16,
    ist: u8,
    attributes: u8,
    offset_middle: u16,
    offset_high: u32,
    reserved: u32,
}

impl IdtEntry {
    const MISSING: Self = Self {
        offset_low: 0,
        selector: 0,
        ist: 0,
        attributes: 0,
        offset_middle: 0,
        offset_high: 0,
        reserved: 0,
    };

    fn interrupt_gate(handler: u64, ist: u8) -> Self {
        Self {
            offset_low: handler as u16,
            selector: KERNEL_CODE_SELECTOR,
            ist: ist & 0x07,
            attributes: 0x8e,
            offset_middle: (handler >> 16) as u16,
            offset_high: (handler >> 32) as u32,
            reserved: 0,
        }
    }
}

#[repr(C, packed)]
struct TaskStateSegment {
    reserved0: u32,
    rsp0: u64,
    rsp1: u64,
    rsp2: u64,
    reserved1: u64,
    ist1: u64,
    ist2: u64,
    ist3: u64,
    ist4: u64,
    ist5: u64,
    ist6: u64,
    ist7: u64,
    reserved2: u64,
    reserved3: u16,
    iomap_base: u16,
}

    const EMPTY: Self = Self {

        rsp0: 0,
        rsp1: 0,
        rsp2: 0,
        reserved1: 0,
        ist1: 0,

        reserved2: 0,
        reserved3: 0,

}

/// Install a private kernel GDT/TSS, exception gates, and device IRQ gates.
///
/// The bootstrap runs with maskable interrupts disabled. This routine leaves
/// them disabled and does not modify CR3 or the inherited page-table hierarchy.
pub fn initialize() {
    // SAFETY: Single-core bootstrap ownership; the descriptor tables are private
    // static storage and are initialized before any gate is loaded.
    unsafe {
        asm!("cli", options(nomem, nostack));
        initialize_tss();
        initialize_gdt();
        initialize_idt();
    }
}

unsafe fn initialize_tss() {
    let ring0_stack = core::ptr::addr_of_mut!(RING0_STACK).cast::<u8>();
    let double_fault_stack = core::ptr::addr_of_mut!(DOUBLE_FAULT_STACK).cast::<u8>();
    // SAFETY: These pointers refer to the ends of distinct, aligned static stacks.
    let ring0_top = unsafe { ring0_stack.add(STACK_SIZE) } as u64;
    // SAFETY: These pointers refer to the ends of distinct, aligned static stacks.
    let double_fault_top = unsafe { double_fault_stack.add(STACK_SIZE) } as u64;
    let tss = core::ptr::addr_of_mut!(TSS);

    // The architectural TSS fields are packed; use unaligned raw writes rather
    // than creating references to their potentially unaligned storage.
    unsafe {
        core::ptr::addr_of_mut!((*tss).rsp0).write_unaligned(ring0_top);
        core::ptr::addr_of_mut!((*tss).ist1).write_unaligned(double_fault_top);
    }
}

unsafe fn initialize_gdt() {
    let tss_base = core::ptr::addr_of!(TSS) as u64;
    let tss_limit = (size_of::<TaskStateSegment>() - 1) as u64;
    let low = (tss_limit & 0xffff)
        | ((tss_base & 0x00ff_ffff) << 16)
        | (TSS_DESCRIPTOR_TYPE << 40)
        | ((tss_limit & 0x000f_0000) << 32)
        | ((tss_base & 0xff00_0000) << 32);
    let high = tss_base >> 32;

    unsafe {
        core::ptr::addr_of_mut!(GDT[0]).write(0);
        core::ptr::addr_of_mut!(GDT[1]).write(0x00af_9a00_0000_ffff);
        core::ptr::addr_of_mut!(GDT[2]).write(0x00cf_9200_0000_ffff);
        core::ptr::addr_of_mut!(GDT[3]).write(low);
        core::ptr::addr_of_mut!(GDT[4]).write(high);
    }

    let gdtr = DescriptorTablePointer {
        limit: (size_of::<[u64; 5]>() - 1) as u16,
        base: core::ptr::addr_of!(GDT) as u64,
    };
    // SAFETY: `GDT` and its TSS descriptor are initialized and remain live.
    unsafe { rustix_load_gdt(&gdtr) };
}

unsafe fn initialize_idt() {
    let idt_entries = core::ptr::addr_of_mut!(IDT.0).cast::<IdtEntry>();
    let stubs = core::ptr::addr_of!(exception_stub_table).cast::<usize>();

    for vector in 0..EXCEPTION_COUNT {
        // SAFETY: The assembly table contains exactly 32 stub addresses.
        let handler = unsafe { stubs.add(vector).read() } as u64;
        let ist = if vector == 8 { 1 } else { 0 };
        // SAFETY: `vector` is bounded by the statically allocated 256-entry IDT.
        unsafe {
            idt_entries
                .add(vector)
                .write(IdtEntry::interrupt_gate(handler, ist));
        }
    }

    let irq_stubs = core::ptr::addr_of!(irq_stub_table).cast::<usize>();
    for vector in IRQ_FIRST_VECTOR..=IRQ_LAST_VECTOR {
        // SAFETY: The assembly table contains one stub for each allocated vector.
        let handler = unsafe { irq_stubs.add(vector - IRQ_FIRST_VECTOR).read() } as u64;
        // SAFETY: `vector` is bounded by the statically allocated 256-entry IDT.
        unsafe {
            idt_entries
                .add(vector)
                .write(IdtEntry::interrupt_gate(handler, 0));
        }
    }
    // SAFETY: The final table entry is the dedicated 0xff spurious-IRQ stub.
    let spurious_handler = unsafe { irq_stubs.add(IRQ_VECTOR_COUNT).read() } as u64;
    // SAFETY: The APIC spurious vector is a valid IDT index.
    unsafe {
        idt_entries
            .add(APIC_SPURIOUS_VECTOR)
            .write(IdtEntry::interrupt_gate(spurious_handler, 0));
    }

    let idtr = DescriptorTablePointer {
        limit: (size_of::<IdtTable>() - 1) as u16,
        base: core::ptr::addr_of!(IDT) as u64,
    };
    // SAFETY: Every architectural exception gate is initialized in static storage.
    unsafe { asm!("lidt [{}]", in(reg) &idtr, options(readonly, nostack, preserves_flags)) };
}

/// Register one callback for an allocated device IRQ vector.
///
/// # Safety
///
/// The caller must keep the IRQ source masked while registering and ensure it
/// is masked whenever this callback is dispatched. The caller must serialize
/// registration against IRQ dispatch on every CPU. `handler` must not allocate,
/// format output, block, or unwind; it runs with IF disabled and owns the EOI.
/// The source must remain masked until all handler state is ready.
#[allow(dead_code)]
pub unsafe fn register_irq_handler(
    vector: u8,
    handler: IrqHandler,
) -> Result<(), IrqRegistrationError> {
    let vector = vector as usize;
    if !(IRQ_FIRST_VECTOR..=IRQ_LAST_VECTOR).contains(&vector) {
        return Err(IrqRegistrationError::InvalidVector);
    }

    let flags: u64;
    // SAFETY: This reads RFLAGS at CPL 0; the temporary push/pop is balanced.
    unsafe {
        asm!("pushfq", "pop {}", out(reg) flags, options(preserves_flags));
    }
    if flags & (1 << 9) != 0 {
        return Err(IrqRegistrationError::InterruptsEnabled);
    }

    // SAFETY: The API contract requires registration to be serialized with IRQ
    // dispatch, and the vector has been checked against the table bounds.
    let slot = unsafe {
        core::ptr::addr_of_mut!(IRQ_HANDLERS)
            .cast::<Option<IrqHandler>>()
            .add(vector)
    };
    // SAFETY: `slot` points into the initialized static callback table.
    if unsafe { slot.read() }.is_some() {
        return Err(IrqRegistrationError::AlreadyRegistered);
    }
    // SAFETY: Registration is serialized by the caller's masking/IF contract.
    unsafe { slot.write(Some(handler)) };
    Ok(())
}

/// Device IRQ target called by the normalized assembly stubs.
#[no_mangle]
pub extern "C" fn rustix_irq_dispatch(vector: u64) {
    if vector == APIC_SPURIOUS_VECTOR as u64 {
        return;
    }

    if !(IRQ_FIRST_VECTOR as u64..=IRQ_LAST_VECTOR as u64).contains(&vector) {
        fatal_irq_halt();
    }

    // SAFETY: Interrupt gates clear IF, and registration's safety contract
    // serializes writes against this read. No mutable reference is created.
    let handler = unsafe {
        core::ptr::addr_of!(IRQ_HANDLERS)
            .cast::<Option<IrqHandler>>()
            .add(vector as usize)
            .read()
    };
    match handler {
        Some(handler) => handler(),
        None => fatal_irq_halt(),
    }
}

fn fatal_irq_halt() -> ! {
    loop {
        // SAFETY: Unknown device interrupts are fatal and must not be retried.
        unsafe { asm!("cli; hlt", options(nomem, nostack)) };
    }
}

/// Fatal exception target called by the assembly stubs.
#[no_mangle]
pub extern "C" fn rustix_exception_dispatch(context: *const ExceptionContext) -> ! {
    // SAFETY: The common assembly stub passes a pointer to its normalized stack
    // frame, which remains live for the duration of this non-returning handler.
    let context = unsafe { &*context };
    crate::kprintln!(
        "KERNEL EXCEPTION: vector {} ({}) error={:#018x} RIP={:#018x}",
        context.vector,
        exception_name(context.vector),
        context.error_code,
        context.rip
    );
    crate::kprintln!(
        "CS={:#06x} SS={:#06x} RFLAGS={:#018x} RSP={:#018x}",
        context.cs,
        context.ss,
        context.rflags,
        context.rsp
    );
    crate::kprintln!(
        "RAX={:#018x} RBX={:#018x} RCX={:#018x}",
        context.rax,
        context.rbx,
        context.rcx
    );
    crate::kprintln!(
        "RDX={:#018x} RSI={:#018x} RDI={:#018x} RBP={:#018x}",
        context.rdx,
        context.rsi,
        context.rdi,
        context.rbp
    );
    crate::kprintln!(
        "R8={:#018x} R9={:#018x} R10={:#018x} R11={:#018x}",
        context.r8,
        context.r9,
        context.r10,
        context.r11
    );
    crate::kprintln!(
        "R12={:#018x} R13={:#018x} R14={:#018x} R15={:#018x}",
        context.r12,
        context.r13,
        context.r14,
        context.r15
    );

    if context.vector == 14 {
        crate::kprintln!(
            "page fault: present={} write={} user={} reserved={} instruction-fetch={}",
            context.error_code & 1 != 0,
            context.error_code & 2 != 0,
            context.error_code & 4 != 0,
            context.error_code & 8 != 0,
            context.error_code & 16 != 0
        );
        let fault_address: u64;
        // SAFETY: Reading CR2 is a privileged x86_64 operation in this handler.
        unsafe {
            asm!("mov {}, cr2", out(reg) fault_address, options(nomem, nostack, preserves_flags))
        };
        crate::kprintln!("page fault address (CR2): {:#018x}", fault_address);
    }

    loop {
        // SAFETY: Fatal exceptions are not recoverable in the current kernel.
        unsafe { asm!("cli; hlt", options(nomem, nostack)) };
    }
}

fn exception_name(vector: u64) -> &'static str {
    match vector {
        0 => "divide error",
        1 => "debug",
        2 => "non-maskable interrupt",
        3 => "breakpoint",
        4 => "overflow",
        5 => "bound range",
        6 => "invalid opcode",
        7 => "device not available",
        8 => "double fault",
        9 => "coprocessor segment overrun",
        10 => "invalid TSS",
        11 => "segment not present",
        12 => "stack-segment fault",
        13 => "general protection fault",
        14 => "page fault",
        16 => "x87 floating-point",
        17 => "alignment check",
        18 => "machine check",
        19 => "SIMD floating-point",
        20 => "virtualization",
        21 => "control protection",
        28 => "hypervisor injection",
        29 => "VMM communication",
        30 => "security exception",
        _ => "reserved or architecture-specific exception",
    }
}
